lead: A reference electrode is a half-cell whose potential stays fixed, so the unknown electrode beside it can be read from a voltmeter. Without one, a single electrode potential cannot be measured, because only differences exist. Two references appear in most syllabi. The calomel electrode uses mercury and mercurous chloride in saturated KCl and sits at +0.241 V vs SHE at 25 °C. The glass electrode uses a thin pH-sensitive bulb and shifts by 0.0592 V per pH unit at 298 K. Both serve in pH meters and potentiometry. Only a few universities teach them in this detail.
prereq: You need 4.1 for single electrode potentials and 4.2 for the Nernst equation.

blocks.text: The standard hydrogen electrode is awkward daily: it needs hydrogen gas and platinised platinum held at 1 bar against 1 M H⁺. A secondary reference electrode instead holds a steady potential that was fixed once against the SHE. Potentiometry uses it as the quiet partner beside the electrode under study (see 4.4). It must pass almost no current, or its own potential drifts.

items: A mercury pool at the bottom, with a platinum wire sealed through the glass for contact.
A paste of mercury and mercurous chloride (calomel, Hg₂Cl₂) spread over the pool.
Potassium chloride solution above the paste; saturated KCl gives the saturated calomel electrode, SCE.
A side tube ending in a porous plug, which forms the junction with the test solution.

blocks.where: E is the electrode potential in volts vs SHE; E° is the standard potential of the Hg₂Cl₂/Hg couple; [Cl⁻] is the chloride concentration in mol L⁻¹; 0.0592 V is 2.303RT/F at 298 K.

blocks.text: Only chloride concentration and temperature enter, so the potential is reproducible. Saturated KCl at 25 °C gives +0.241 V vs SHE. That is the value exams mean unless another concentration is stated.

A thin bulb of pH-sensitive glass, roughly 0.1 mm thick, seals the end of a tube. Inside sit 0.1 M HCl and a silver wire coated with AgCl — a small Ag/AgCl electrode acting as the inner reference. When the bulb dips into the test solution, H⁺ ions exchange with the hydrated gel layer on the glass surface and build a potential difference across the membrane.

blocks.where: E(glass) is the membrane potential in volts; E°(glass) is a constant for that particular bulb; pH = −log[H⁺]; 0.0592 V is the slope at 298 K, so one pH unit changes the reading by 59.2 mV.

blocks.text: In use the bulb is paired with an SCE: glass | test solution || KCl (saturated) | Hg₂Cl₂, Hg. The cell EMF follows pH in a straight line, and the meter is calibrated with two buffer solutions of known pH before a reading is trusted.

Advantages: nothing is added to the sample, oxidising and coloured solutions are fine, and the range is about pH 1 to 12. Limits: the bulb is fragile and its resistance is very high, so the meter must draw almost no current.

figure.caption: Two secondary reference electrodes and their parts. The calomel unit's fixed potential comes from saturated KCl, while the glass unit senses the test solution through its thin bulb.

spec.aria: A tree splits reference electrodes into calomel, with mercury paste, saturated potassium chloride and a porous plug, and glass, with a glass membrane, internal acid and a silver-silver chloride wire.

examples.question: A saturated calomel electrode has a potential of +0.241 V vs SHE. It is coupled with a copper electrode dipping into 1 M Cu²⁺, and copper is the cathode. The voltmeter reads 0.099 V. Find the potential of the copper electrode vs SHE.
steps: For a cell, EMF = E(cathode) − E(anode).
Copper is the cathode, so EMF = E(Cu) − E(SCE).
Rearrange: E(Cu) = 0.099 V + 0.241 V = 0.340 V vs SHE.
Check against the standard value for Cu²⁺/Cu, about +0.34 V — the sign and size agree.
examples.answer: The copper electrode potential is +0.340 V vs SHE.
examples.check:
e_sce = 0.241
emf = 0.099
e_cu = emf + e_sce
print(f"{e_cu:.3f}")

traps: Do not set the saturated calomel electrode at 0.00 V. Zero belongs to the standard hydrogen electrode; the SCE is about +0.241 V vs SHE at 25 °C.
The SCE potential shifts with KCl concentration and with temperature, so a quoted 0.241 V is for saturated KCl at 25 °C only.
Sign slip: EMF = E(cathode) − E(anode). Fix which electrode is the cathode before adding or subtracting the reference potential.
The glass electrode slope is 0.0592 V per pH unit at 298 K, not 0.0592 mV, and the slope itself changes with temperature.
Calomel is the reference; glass is the indicator. In a pH cell the glass bulb is the electrode that responds to the sample, and the SCE only holds the other end steady.

quiz.q: Why is a reference electrode needed in potentiometry?
quiz.a: Only potential differences can be measured. A fixed known half-cell gives a second point of comparison, so the unknown single electrode potential can be found from the cell EMF.

quiz.q: Write the half-reaction at the calomel electrode and state its potential for saturated KCl at 25 °C.
Why is saturated KCl used in the calomel electrode rather than a dilute solution?
quiz.a: A fixed, high chloride concentration keeps [Cl⁻] constant, so the Nernst term stays constant and the potential is reproducible. Saturation also lowers the cell resistance and, since K⁺ and Cl⁻ move at similar speeds, keeps the liquid junction potential small.

quiz.q: A glass electrode cell is calibrated at pH 4.0 and reads a sample at pH 7.0. By how much does the cell EMF change at 298 K?
quiz.a: ΔpH = 7.0 − 4.0 = 3.0 units. Change = 3.0 × 0.0592 V = 0.1776 V ≈ 0.178 V, with the glass electrode becoming more negative as pH rises.

quiz.q: An electrode is made the cathode against an SCE and the voltmeter reads 0.150 V. Find its potential vs SHE.
quiz.a: EMF = E(cathode) − E(SCE), so E = 0.150 V + 0.241 V = 0.391 V vs SHE.

quiz.q: Why must a pH meter used with a glass electrode have a very high input impedance?
quiz.a: The thin glass bulb has a resistance of the order of 10⁸ Ω. A meter of low impedance would draw current, cause polarisation at the electrodes and give a wrong or drifting EMF; high impedance keeps the current near zero so the measured EMF is the true open-circuit value.

quiz.q: A student stores the SCE dry and later gets unstable readings. Explain the likely cause.
quiz.a: Drying blocks the porous plug and lets the KCl concentration at the junction fall below saturation, so the chloride term and the junction potential both change. The electrode must be kept in saturated KCl so the plug stays wet and the potential stays at +0.241 V.

beyond: Not for the exam. Working pH meters use a combination electrode: the glass bulb and an Ag/AgCl reference sit in one body, which is why a single probe has two connectors or one BNC plug. Silver-silver chloride references have largely replaced calomel in commercial instruments because mercury waste is restricted and Ag/AgCl is compact. The same membrane idea extends to ion-selective electrodes for F⁻, Ca²⁺, K⁺ and nitrate in water testing. Junction potential and reference drift are the practical accuracy limits of any such measurement. Search for combination pH electrode construction, Ag/AgCl reference, and ion-selective electrode to go further.
